name: Mercury oxide
plain: An old 1.35-volt type with a very steady voltage, once used in instruments and light meters. It contains mercury, and its sale is banned in many countries.
cathode: Mercury(II) oxide with graphite, sometimes mixed with manganese dioxide
summary: Mercury oxide cells, also called mercury or Ruben-Mallory cells, paired a zinc anode with a mercuric oxide cathode and held an almost constant 1.35 V until nearly exhausted. Their mercury content led to sales bans from the 1990s, and ANSI and IEC have withdrawn their standards.
body:
## How it works

A mercury cell uses a zinc anode, a cathode of mercury(II) oxide, and an alkaline electrolyte of sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide. Mercuric oxide does not conduct, so graphite is mixed into the cathode; the graphite also keeps the reduced mercury from collecting into large droplets. A paper or other porous separator soaked in electrolyte divides the electrodes. The overall reaction is Zn + HgO → ZnO + Hg: zinc oxidizes to zinc oxide and mercuric oxide is reduced to elemental mercury. Cells carry a little extra mercuric oxide to prevent hydrogen gas from forming at end of life.

## Discharge behavior

The discharge curve is very flat. Wikipedia describes a constant 1.35 V until about the last 5% of life, then a rapid drop, with voltage held within 1% for several years at light load and over a wide temperature range. That stability made the cells useful as voltage references in instruments and in photographic light meters. Cells with a cathode of mercuric oxide mixed with manganese dioxide gave 1.4 V on a more sloped curve; IEC listed that variant separately as system N. Sodium hydroxide cells held nearly constant voltage at low currents, for hearing aids, calculators and watches, while potassium hydroxide cells held voltage at higher currents, for cameras with flash and backlit watches. A mercuric oxide and cadmium variant ran near 0.9 V but tolerated temperatures up to 180 °C in special designs.

## Uses

Military equipment during and after World War II, then hearing aids, watches, calculators, cameras and light meters. The sales bans caused problems for photographers whose equipment relied on the flat discharge curve. Substitutes include zinc-air cells, which have a similar flat curve but a life of a few months and poor performance in dry climates, alkaline cells with a sloping voltage, and silver oxide cells, which run at a higher voltage. Adapters with Schottky or germanium diodes drop silver oxide voltage closer to 1.35 V, though the drop varies with current.

## History

The mercury oxide and zinc couple was known in the 19th century but saw little use until 1942, when Samuel Ruben developed a balanced cell for military uses such as metal detectors, munitions and walkie-talkies. EU Directive 91/157 (1991) restricted batteries containing more than 25 mg of mercury, and in 1998 the limit fell to 0.005% by weight. New Jersey prohibited mercury battery sales in 1992. In 1996 the US Mercury-Containing and Rechargeable Battery Management Act prohibited further sale of mercury-containing batteries, with an exception of up to 25 mg of mercury per button cell. Directive 2013/56/EU ended the EU button cell exemption on October 1, 2015, leaving a 0.0005% mercury limit for all batteries.

## Status

Obsolete. ANSI and IEC have withdrawn their mercury battery standards; IEC 60086-1 letters M (mercuric oxide) and N (mercuric oxide with manganese dioxide) are listed as withdrawn.
strengths: Very flat 1.35 V discharge until about the last 5% of life
Voltage stable enough to serve as a reference in instruments and light meters
Long shelf life, up to 10 years (Wikipedia)
limitations: Contains mercury; sale is banned in many countries
Standards withdrawn by ANSI and IEC
safety: Mercury content is toxic and an environmental hazard at disposal
